reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / WHO Classification of Skin Tumours
clinicalPearls: Typically presents as a rapidly enlarging, painless, firm violaceous or red nodule on sun-exposed skin of elderly or immunosuppressed patients
The acronym AEIOU (Asymptomatic, Expanding rapidly, Immunosuppression, Older than fifty, UV-exposed fair skin) captures the classic clinical profile
Two distinct pathways exist: a Merkel-cell polyomavirus-driven form and a UV-mutagenesis-driven form with high tumour mutational burden
Histology shows small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm, salt-and-pepper chromatin, and a high mitotic and apoptotic rate
Immunohistochemistry demonstrates a characteristic paranuclear dot pattern of cytokeratin 20 and neuroendocrine markers, with negativity for TTF-1 helping exclude metastatic small-cell lung carcinoma
Early regional nodal spread is common, so sentinel lymph node biopsy is central to staging even in clinically node-negative disease
Management combines wide local excision (or Mohs micrographic surgery) with adjuvant radiotherapy, and immune-checkpoint inhibition has transformed treatment of advanced disease
The tumour is markedly more common and more aggressive in the immunosuppressed, including transplant recipients and those with HIV or haematological malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Merkel cell carcinoma is an aggressive cutaneous neuroendocrine malignancy that arises through two convergent routes. In roughly the majority of cases in many populations, clonal integration of Merkel-cell polyomavirus into the host genome, together with truncating mutations of the viral large T antigen, drives persistent expression of viral oncoproteins that inactivate tumour-suppressor pathways such as retinoblastoma protein signalling. The alternative route is chronic ultraviolet damage producing a very high burden of somatic mutations, typically in virus-negative tumours. Both pathways yield a proliferation of small cells with neuroendocrine differentiation that infiltrate the dermis, invade lymphatics readily, and metastasise early to regional nodes and beyond. The strong influence of immune surveillance explains both the excess incidence in immunosuppression and the notable responsiveness to checkpoint blockade.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic small-cell lung carcinoma to skin
Cutaneous lymphoma (including lymphoblastic and other small round cell infiltrates)
Basal cell carcinoma, particularly nodular type
Cutaneous metastasis from other neuroendocrine primaries
Ewing sarcoma / peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumour of skin
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histopathology for small round blue cell morphology
Immunohistochemistry panel including cytokeratin 20 (paranuclear dot), neuroendocrine markers, and TTF-1 to exclude pulmonary origin
Sentinel lymph node biopsy for regional staging in clinically node-negative disease
Cross-sectional imaging or functional imaging to assess nodal and distant metastasis
Merkel-cell polyomavirus status or oncoprotein antibody testing where available for prognostication and surveillance
Assessment of immune status including consideration of underlying immunosuppression or occult malignancy
redFlags: Rapidly growing painless nodule on sun-exposed skin of an older or immunosuppressed patient
Palpable regional lymphadenopathy suggesting nodal metastasis
In-transit cutaneous satellite lesions indicating aggressive lymphatic spread
Systemic symptoms or imaging findings suggesting distant metastatic disease
New aggressive skin tumour in a transplant recipient or other profoundly immunosuppressed individual
reference.prognosis: Merkel cell carcinoma is aggressive with a substantial risk of nodal and distant metastasis; outcome is strongly stage-dependent, being relatively favourable for small localised node-negative lesions but poor once regional or distant spread occurs. Immunosuppression worsens prognosis, while immune-checkpoint inhibition has meaningfully improved survival in advanced disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking the bland-looking nodule for a benign cyst or lipoma and delaying biopsy
Failing to perform immunohistochemistry to distinguish it from metastatic small-cell lung carcinoma and other small round cell tumours
Omitting sentinel lymph node biopsy in clinically node-negative disease and thereby understaging
Underestimating aggressiveness in immunosuppressed patients or attributing rapid growth to a benign process
management: Perform baseline workup with full skin and nodal exam, blood counts, liver function tests, and cross-sectional or PET imaging to assess regional and distant spread, since MCC has a strong tendency toward local recurrence, nodal spread, and metastasis.
Treat localized disease with complete surgical excision, typically wide local excision with margins in the 1 to 2 cm range, as the mainstay approach.
Consider Mohs micrographic surgery as an alternative to wide local excision in cosmetically sensitive sites, with local control that appears comparable though less well studied.

Perform sentinel lymph node biopsy in clinically and radiologically node-negative disease to avoid understaging, and sequence it before or alongside definitive excision rather than after, so the surgery does not alter lymphatic drainage.

Discuss regional nodal disease at multidisciplinary tumor board to decide between completion lymph node dissection and nodal radiotherapy, as outcomes appear broadly similar between the two approaches.
Offer adjuvant nodal radiotherapy to patients who decline or are not candidates for sentinel node biopsy.
Consider adjuvant radiotherapy to the primary site for tumors at significant risk of local recurrence or with positive margins, reflecting the tumor's radiosensitivity.

Reserve radiation alone, without surgery, for patients who are not surgical candidates, recognizing it controls the site less reliably and carries a higher risk of distant recurrence than complete resection.
Use PD-1 or PD-L1 checkpoint immunotherapy as first-line, standard-of-care systemic treatment for metastatic or unresectable disease, with better response rates in treatment-naive patients.

Reserve cytotoxic chemotherapy, using regimens modeled on small-cell lung carcinoma treatment, mainly for palliation in patients not eligible for or who have progressed on checkpoint immunotherapy, since it has not shown a survival benefit.
Consider neoadjuvant checkpoint immunotherapy before surgery for resectable disease as an investigational approach with promising early pathologic response data, pending larger comparative trials.
Follow up with skin and lymph node exams every few months for the first two to three years, spacing out to annual or semiannual visits thereafter given the high recurrence risk.

Track Merkel cell polyomavirus oncoprotein antibody titers on surveillance when previously elevated, since a rising titer has reasonably strong predictive value for recurrence and can prompt earlier imaging.

Address immunosuppression where feasible and evaluate for underlying immunosuppressive conditions such as HIV, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, or transplant status, given how strongly immune status drives this cancer's risk and behavior.
